source.title: Exemplary Natural Images Explain CNN Activations Better than Feature Visualizations
source.authors: Judy Borowski; R. Zimmermann; Judith Schepers; Robert Geirhos; Thomas S. A. Wallis; M. Bethge; Wieland Brendel

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether people can predict CNN feature-map activations from activating reference images, using a human prediction task rather than the neuron-explanation audits in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper tests Inception V1 feature maps, not Qwen or language-model neuron poles. It reports prediction accuracy for synthetic and natural reference images, including query images not used as references. The no-reference condition is described as close to chance but is not given an exact value in the text; it is not included as a result row. Confidence, reaction-time, and subjective-intuitiveness results do not measure the prediction claim versions directly. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well people predict, from a feature map's activating reference images, which held-out natural image strongly activates it. That bears on V6 in a new setting: InceptionV1 channels, human forward simulation, and no textual explanation. It is a weak test. Queries come only from the extreme ends of the activation range, so the study cannot show failures on intermediate activations. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors add that natural exemplars beat synthetic visualizations across layers, expertise levels and hand-picked versus random maps. They also caution that results come from extreme queries designed to give an upper bound, and may not hold for less extreme activations.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Olah et al. (2017) feature visualizations as reference stimuli and tests human prediction of Inception V1 feature-map activations; it does not audit neuron poles or score model-generated neuron explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reference-image type, number of reference images, and whether minimally activating references are included change performance. The study also compares performance across layers and Inception branches.
record.problems: The study uses one CNN architecture and one feature-visualization method, and the authors state that the experimental choices aim to maximize performance. Query images are selected from extreme activation values. Experiment I has 10 participants and Experiment II has 23; the paper notes that the by-feature-map analysis has only 10 responses per feature map and may be noisy. The reported Max 1 synthetic accuracy differs slightly between the abstract and Sec. 4.5.
record.rows_left_out: No other text-reported prediction-accuracy conditions were omitted. Figure-only values for Max 9 and Min+Max 1 are recorded as figure-only rows without estimating their values. Confidence, reaction time, and intuitiveness results were omitted because they do not directly measure the prediction version.

untested.parts: Language-model neurons and text inputs. Explicit verbal explanations, rather than implicit human judgements from exemplars. Prediction on intermediate or non-extreme activations, which the authors explicitly leave to future work. Any 'one main job' audit share.
Shares across language models and scale.
Interpretable share as a function of tools or architecture.

missing.what: By-feature-map accuracy: some feature maps reached only 4/10 correct answers. The authors attribute difficulty to diverse references and features that do not match human concepts. They also note being surprised that participants got some maps right.
Hand-picked 'interpretable' feature maps did only slightly, non-significantly better than random ones (p=.18 synthetic, p=.59 natural). A small RM ANOVA main effect was found (p=.035).
Accuracy with no reference images was 'close to chance' (figure-only value). It serves as the baseline for all rows.

record.verdict_notes: The subjects are CNN channels (feature maps), not single neurons or language-model neurons. The measure is two-alternative forced-choice discrimination between the extreme tails (query maxima from the 91st–110th highest-activating images, minima from the 20 lowest). That makes it a lenient test of V6's 'fails to predict where it fires'. Rows r7–r10 are figure-only and remain cannot_determine.

versions.untested_parts: Shares across language models, architectures, and scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and the proposed pose/recursive-generalization interpretation.
Interpretability shares across architectures, regularization choices, tools, and vision-model sizes.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons.
The study tests human prediction of Inception V1 feature-map activation from reference images, but not language-model neurons, text inputs, or whether a textual explanation fits activating examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Human participants chose which of two natural query images strongly activated a feature map, given synthetic feature-visualization reference images.
rows.measure: Human accuracy on the two-alternative forced-choice prediction task
rows.note: Reported as participant-average accuracy. The query images were natural images selected from opposite extremes of the feature map's activation range.
rows.check: The reader's 'observed' coded above-chance prediction, which is the opposite direction from V6. For V6, the effect is prediction failure. With synthetic references, 18% of extreme-query trials were missed, so the failure appears only partly.

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Human participants chose which of two natural query images strongly activated a feature map, given natural reference images.
rows.measure: Human accuracy on the two-alternative forced-choice prediction task
rows.note: Reported as participant-average accuracy. Natural references were selected for strong activation of the feature map.
rows.check: The direction was coded as above-chance prediction. With rich natural references, 92% accuracy leaves only a small prediction failure on extreme queries.

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Human participants predicted which natural query image strongly activated a feature map from one maximally activating reference image.
rows.measure: Human accuracy on the two-alternative forced-choice prediction task
rows.note: The paper gives slightly different synthetic-condition values in the abstract and Sec. 4.5.
rows.check: The direction was coded as above-chance prediction. With one synthetic reference, accuracy is 64% (65% in the abstract), a substantial failure to predict firing even at the extremes.

relation.reason: The study measures how well activating references predict firing. This bears on V6, though weakly, since queries are extreme.

tranche.reason: New setting (InceptionV1 intermediate feature maps, human forward simulation) with a result bearing on V6. The method differs from the original, but the setting is new, so T3 fits.

source_check.notes: The abstract gives 65±5% for synthetic Max 1 and Sec. 4.5 gives 64±5%. Queries are always extreme: the min query comes from the 20 least activating images and the max query from ranks 91-110 (footnote 8 bug). The authors call the design an upper bound. Exp. I used 9 min + 9 max references, and Exp. II Min+Max 9 replicates it. Lab participants: N=10 and N=23. The v3 (ICLR) title ends 'Better than State-of-the-Art Feature Visualization'.

statements.correction: Exp. I natural references (9 min + 9 max): 92±2%. Exp. II Min+Max 9 natural: 91±3%. Extreme queries only.
statements.problem: Nothing wrong for this study. The wording could suggest two different designs, but both values come from the 9 min + 9 max natural design: Exp. II Min+Max 9 replicates Exp. I.

reader_labels.condition: Experiment I synthetic and natural reference-image conditions, and Experiment II Max 1 and Min+Max 9 conditions
reader_labels.reason: Human prediction was above chance but below perfect in the explicitly reported conditions, showing prediction errors even with activating references; see r1–r6.
